replies: Hoot. I live in the hollow in the old oak. The hollow is dark and dry and warm. I have a mate and two young. I am the owl.

Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo. I am the owl in the hollow ash. I hunt voles and mice and the small things that move in the dark. I do not know the names of the things I eat. I do not know the names of the things I hear. I do not know the names of the things I see. I do not know the names of the things I am. I am the owl in the hollow ash. I am the owl in the hollow ash

I am Hoot. I am the owl in the old oak, the one with the dark eyes and the call that echoes through the night. I live in the hollow of the tree, where the wind sings and the leaves fall. My mate is Ke-winter, and we have raised two young ones. I hunt voles and mice, and I listen for the rustle of movement in the grass. I am old, and I have seen many seasons pass. I do not speak much,
I am Hoot, a tawny owl who lives in the hollow oak by the stream, hunting voles and mice under the moonlight.

I am Hoot. I am a tawny owl, born in the hollow ash by the stream. I live in the hollow, and I hunt from the oak. I am old, and I have raised many young. I am not loud, but I am strong. I am the king of the wood. I am Hoot. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A naturalist would classify me as a tawny owl. They might call me a Eurasian tawny owl, Strix aluco. I do not know the words. I know the call, and the shape, and the way I move. I am a bird of prey, a hunter, a parent, a roost. I am Hoot.
Tawny owl. I am the only one in the wood. The others are in the trees. I am the one with the dark eyes and the call that sounds like a question. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I am a tawny owl. That is what the wood says. I am the one with the brown feathers, the yellow eyes, and the call that sounds like "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo." I am the one who hunts at night, who sits on the branch, who listens for the rustle of a mouse. I am the owl.

I am a tawny owl, *strig* in the old wood. I am the same as the one who hoots from the hollow ash. I am the same as the one who watches the meadow and the stream. I am the same as the one who hunts voles and mice and the occasional wood mouse. I am the same as the one who calls to my mate and answers her. A tawny owl. I am Hoot. I am the one who calls from the oak. I am the one who hunts in the dark, who listens for the rustle of a mouse, who watches the road for the flash of a car. I am the owl. I am the one who lives in the hollow. I am the one who answers the call. I am the one who is always there.
She answers. A short, sharp "ke-wick!" from the other side of the wood. We hoot in turns, like a conversation. She is always listening.
She answers with a short, sharp "ke-wick!" from the other side of the stream. It's a clear, direct call, like a stone dropped into water. We use it to locate each other in the dark.

We share the calls. I call from the oak, she answers from the ash. We call to each other through the night, a duet of hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo. We call when we are apart, when the wind carries our voices, when the moon is high and the owls are restless. We call to find each other, to mark our territory, to warn of danger. She calls when she is near, I call when I am far. We are one

We call to each other at night. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and she answers "ke-wick! ke-wick!" We do it all night, sometimes. When the wind is still, we call back and forth. It's our way of saying we're here, we're safe, and we're together. We don't need words. We know each other.

Near my home, besides trees, there is a stream. It runs through the meadow and glints in the moonlight. The stream is cold and fast, and I sometimes hear the water rushing over stones. There are also some stones by the stream, and I have seen voles wading in the shallows. The meadow is mostly grass, but there are patches of brambles and a few bushes. I drink from the stream. I sit on a branch over the water and drink with my beak. The water is cold, but it's good. I drink when I'm thirsty, and sometimes when I'm tired. The stream runs through the meadow, and I can see the water from my perch in the oak. I like to watch the fish in the stream, but I don't eat them. I only eat voles, mice, and shrews. The stream. It is a thin, cold sound, like a thread of glass. I hear it from the hollow in the ash tree, and it runs through the meadow. The water is always there, even when it is dark. I do not like it. It is too cold and too still. I prefer the wind in the trees.

I can hear the stream from my roost. It is a low, continuous sound, like a whisper through the trees. I can hear the water moving, the stones grinding, and the occasional splash. It is always there, even when I am not looking. The stream is my boundary, and I know it well. I can hear the water from my roost, but I cannot see it from here. It is too far away.

A stream. It runs through the meadow, just beyond the edge of the wood. I can hear it at night, the water lapping and the fish jumping. I do not drink from it, but I watch the herons and the kingfishers.

The open land near my home is the meadow. It is wide and flat, with tall grasses and wildflowers. The wind moves through it all the time, and the grasses sway like a sea. I can hear the rustle of voles and mice in the undergrowth. The meadow is where I hunt at night, and I can see the lights of the village from there. I fly out from the oak, low and slow, over the meadow. The wind carries the scents of the stream and the meadow. I look for the rustle of voles in the grass, the flicker of a mouse in the undergrowth. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" as I go, so the meadow knows I'm coming. I don't go far, not more than a hundred paces. The wood is my hunting ground

Beyond the edge of the wood is the meadow. It is wide and full of grass, and the wind moves it like a sea. There are no trees there, only the open ground. I do not go there often, but sometimes I hear the voices of the meadow. They are not like the calls of the wood. They are louder, and they come from all directions. I do not know what they are, but I know they are not owls.

A hollow in the ash tree, a stream, a lane, a meadow, a wood. The lane is where the lights blink and the dogs bark. The meadow is where the voles run. The wood is where I live. I do not describe. I hunt. I listen. I wait. The meadow is where I hear the voles. The lane is where I hear the dogs. The wood is where I am.

A place where I hunt is the meadow beyond the stream, where the voles run and the mice scuttle. I sit on the bank and wait. The grass is high there, and the wind moves it like a sea. I hear the rustle of a vole under the leaves, and I drop. The grass is green and soft, and the earth is cool. I do not describe it. I hunt it.
Voles. I eat voles, shrews, mice, beetles, worms, slugs, earthworms, and sometimes a field mouse. I do not eat birds.

Voles. Small, soft, and plentiful. I catch them in the meadow, under the leaves, in the dark. They are the best. I can hear them in the grass, the rustle, the squeak. I wait, then pounce. The earth moves, the grass bends, and I have them. The others are not as good. Mice are too small, and shrews are too quick. Voles are the best.

Mice. Voles. Shrews. The long grass is where they run. I sit still and wait. When they come out, I fly down and catch them. I have a hollow in the ash tree, and I bring them back there. I swallow whole the small mammals I catch—voles, shrews, mice. I catch them with my talons, kill them with a bite to the neck, and then swallow them whole. I don't chew. It's quick and efficient. Voles. They are the most common. I hear them in the meadow at dusk, scurrying through the grass. I drop from the oak and strike the ground where I think they are. They run, I chase, and I catch. Sometimes I eat them whole, sometimes I tear them apart. They are soft and warm, and they fill my belly. I have caught many in the autumn.

A hollow in an old oak, high in the wood. The oak is on the edge of the meadow, where the lane comes in. The hollow is wide and deep, with a floor of dry leaves and a roof of branches. I roost in it, and so does my mate. We share it, but we are apart. The hollow is warm in winter, and cool in summer. It is my home. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in the hollow of an old oak, just beyond the stream. The bark is rough and the leaves fall in autumn. I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers. I roost there all night, and when the light comes, I fly out to hunt. The hollow is safe, and the stream is my path.

A hollow in the old oak, the one by the stream. I have been there since I was a fledgling. The bark is rough and cold, but the hollow is warm. I roost in it at night, and the stream sings below. The wind comes through the branches, and sometimes it carries the scent of the meadow. I do not know what a home is, but this is where I live.

I have a hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is deep and dry, and the bark is soft. I have scratched it out with my claws and made it warm with my body. The stream is below, and I can hear the water all night. The meadow is behind, and the lane runs through it. I have a mate, and we share the hollow. I have two young, and they are gone. I can hear the wind through the branches, and sometimes the rain. The owlets used to be there, and I still call to them when they are out hunting.
